questions.p:
Aisha, 16, has had heavy periods since menarche and nosebleeds that last over 30 minutes. Her father bruises easily. She takes no drugs.

Hb 104 g/L (ref 115-160)
Platelets 230 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR normal
aPTT mildly prolonged
vWF antigen 0.6 IU/mL
vWF activity 0.2 IU/mL
FVIII activity mildly low

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: B. vWF activity is a third of the antigen, well under 70%, so the vWF that is present doesn't work. That is a qualitative defect, type 2 VWD.
A: Glanzmann thrombasthenia has normal vWF.
C: Type 3 has almost no vWF at all.
D: Type 1 lowers antigen and activity in proportion.
E: Hemophilia A is X-linked and causes joint and muscle bleeds.
Takeaway: Type 2 has 4 subtypes: 2A, 2B, 2M and 2N.

questions.p: Which of the following is NOT part of ITP management?
o: Glucocorticoids such as prednisone or dexamethasone
questions.e:
Correct: C. Plasma exchange to replace ADAMTS-13 treats TTP.
A: Rituximab is an ITP treatment (and also used in TTP).
B: TPO mimetics (romiplostim, eltrombopag) are an ITP treatment.
D: Glucocorticoids are an ITP treatment.
Takeaway: ITP: steroids, IVIg, splenectomy, rituximab, TPO mimetics, immune suppression.

questions.p:
Two patients present.
Patient 1: recurrent nosebleeds, heavy periods, easy bruising.
Patient 2: spontaneous swelling of the knee and a thigh hematoma.

Which category of defect does each pattern suggest, in order?
questions.e:
Correct: D. Mucocutaneous bleeding suggests platelets or vWF. Deep bleeding into joints and muscles suggests coagulation factor deficiency.
A: This reverses the patterns.
B: Hyperfibrinolysis is not suggested, and joints point to factors.
C: Joint and muscle bleeds point to coagulation factors.
Takeaway: Primary = mucocutaneous, often immediate. Secondary = deep, less immediate.

questions.p: A 6-day-old boy who received vitamin K at birth oozes from his umbilical stump. Platelets, PT, aPTT and fibrinogen are all normal. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.e:
Correct: A. FXIII cross-links fibrin after the clot forms, so PT and aPTT stay normal. Neonatal umbilical bleeding and ICH are classic FXIII presentations.
B: FVII deficiency gives an isolated prolonged PT.
C: Hemophilia A prolongs the aPTT.
D: He received vitamin K, and deficiency prolongs the PT.
Takeaway: Bleeding with normal INR and PTT: remember FXIII deficiency.

questions.p:
Three people complete standardized bleeding tools.
Patient 1: woman, 30, ISTH BAT 5
Patient 2: man, 30, ISTH BAT 5
Patient 3: child, 9, PBQ 3

How should each score be interpreted, in order?
questions.e:
Correct: C. ISTH BAT normal cut-offs are under 4 in adult males and under 6 in adult females. PBQ is positive above 2.
A: The woman's 5 is under 6, so it is normal.
B: This reverses the sex-specific cut-offs, and PBQ 3 is positive.
D: The man's 5 is above his cut-off, and a PBQ of 3 is positive.
Takeaway: A normal BAT has a high negative predictive value for a mild bleeding disorder.

questions.p: Which statement about fibrinolysis (tertiary hemostasis) is correct?
o: t-PA converts fibrinogen into fibrin monomers
D-dimers form when thrombin cleaves soluble fibrin
PAI-1 activates t-PA to speed clot breakdown
TAFI inhibits plasmin formation and suppresses fibrinolysis
questions.e:
Correct: D. TAFI (thrombin activatable fibrinolysis inhibitor) inhibits formation of plasmin.
A: Thrombin, not t-PA, converts fibrinogen to fibrin. t-PA converts plasminogen to plasmin.
B: D-dimers come from plasmin acting on cross-linked fibrin.
C: PAI-1 inhibits t-PA. It slows breakdown.
Takeaway: t-PA makes plasmin. Plasmin makes D-dimers. TAFI, PAI-1 and antiplasmin apply the brakes.

questions.p:
Jordan, 40, had a CBC for a work medical. He feels well and has never had bruising, nosebleeds or bleeding after dental work or a past appendectomy. He takes no drugs. His exam is normal.

Hb 148 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 6.9 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 35 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR normal
aPTT normal
Sample: lavender top tube
Film: large platelet clumps.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. No bleeding ever, a normal exam, an EDTA tube and platelet clumps on the film fit pseudothrombocytopenia. Antibodies bind platelets in EDTA, and the counter misses the clumps.
A: Bernard Soulier causes bleeding.
B: TTP brings hemolysis and a sick patient.
C: ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion and shows no clumps.
D: Sequestration needs a large spleen.
Takeaway: Repeat the count in a sodium citrate tube.

questions.p:
Ethan, 4, has new petechiae on his legs and two nosebleeds. Two weeks ago he had a cold. He is playing happily and has no fever, bone pain, weight loss or bloody diarrhea. On exam he has scattered petechiae and bruises, with no enlarged nodes, liver or spleen.

Hb 124 g/L (ref 110-140)
WBC 7.6 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Neutrophils and lymphocytes normal
Platelets 8 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR normal
aPTT normal
Film: a few large platelets. No blasts, no schistocytes, no clumps.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. A well child with isolated severe thrombocytopenia after a viral illness, other cell lines normal and a clean film fits ITP, a diagnosis of exclusion. Half of cases are children, and these resolve within 6 months.
A: HUS follows bloody diarrhea, with hemolysis and kidney injury.
B: Pseudothrombocytopenia shows clumps and causes no bleeding.
C: ALL lowers other cell lines and shows blasts.
D: TTP brings hemolytic anemia, schistocytes and neurological signs.
Takeaway: ITP: antibodies coat platelets, and splenic macrophages consume them.

questions.p:
Kofi, 50, is in the ICU with septic shock from pneumonia. Over 12 hours he has started oozing from IV sites and his central line, with new bruises. He has had no heparin.

Hb 85 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 22 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 40 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR 2.0
aPTT prolonged
Fibrinogen 0.8 g/L
D-dimer very high
Film: schistocytes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: A. Sepsis with bleeding, platelets under 100, a high INR, fibrinogen under 1 g/L, a high D-dimer and schistocytes fit DIC. Overactive clotting consumes factors and platelets.
B: TTP has a normal INR and fibrinogen.
C: Vitamin K deficiency leaves platelets and fibrinogen normal.
D: HIT needs heparin and causes clots, not oozing.
E: ITP has normal clotting tests.
Takeaway: DIC: cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen is under 1.0 g/L, platelets if under 50, plasma if INR over 1.5.

questions.p: Which patient best meets an indication for red cell transfusion?
o: Hb 78 g/L, age 25, no symptoms or cardiac history
Hb 85 g/L, age 70, coronary disease, chest pain
Hb 95 g/L in a 50 year old before elective surgery
Hb 72 g/L, age 40, refuses blood products
questions.e:
Correct: B. Hb 70 to 90 g/L with risk of cardiac ischemia is an indication.
A: Without symptoms or cardiac risk, the threshold is under 70.
C: 95 is above the listed thresholds.
D: Patient refusal is a contraindication. Consider EPO, iron, B12 and folate.
Takeaway: 1 unit RBC raises Hb by about 10 g/L.

questions.p: Which patient meets an indication for platelet transfusion?
o: A patient with TTP, platelets 15 x 10^9/L and no bleeding
A patient with HIT and platelets 40 x 10^9/L
A stable outpatient with platelets 25 x 10^9/L and no bleeding
A patient with platelets 80 x 10^9/L going for neurosurgery
questions.e:
Correct: D. Neurosurgery needs platelets above 100 x 10^9/L.
A: TTP is a contraindication because it fuels further thrombosis.
B: HIT is a contraindication.
C: Prophylactic transfusion without bleeding or a procedure targets under 10.
Takeaway: Platelet thresholds: under 10, under 50 for invasive surgery, under 100 for neurosurgery.

questions.p:
George, 81, had hip fracture surgery yesterday. He had a DVT 5 years ago.

How long should his thromboprophylaxis last at minimum?
questions.e:
Correct: C. Hip fracture is the highest VTE risk. Prophylaxis runs at least 7 to 10 days, extended to 4 to 6 weeks with cancer or past VTE.
A: Prophylaxis is time limited.
B: 7 to 10 days applies without cancer or prior VTE.
D: Prophylaxis continues while he is not ambulatory and beyond discharge.
Takeaway: Virchow's triad: stasis, injury, hypercoagulability.

questions.p: Which blood product is correctly paired with its storage?
o: Plasma: 4 °C in the blood bank fridge, up to 1 year
Platelets: 20 to 24 °C with mixing, up to 7 days
Red cells: room temperature, up to 42 days
Cryoprecipitate: room temperature, up to 5 years
questions.e:
Correct: B. Platelets stay at room temperature with constant slow mixing to preserve function, up to 7 days.
A: Plasma is frozen at -18 °C for up to 1 year.
C: Red cells are refrigerated at 4 °C for up to 42 days.
D: Cryo is frozen at -18 °C for up to 1 year.
Takeaway: Fibrinogen concentrate and PCCs are lyophilized with virus inactivation.

questions.p:
Hector, 61, has early satiety and fullness in his left upper abdomen. Ultrasound shows a spleen of 18 cm. His liver enzymes and liver function are normal. He has no bleeding.

Hb 118 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 3.6 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 70 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR normal
Reticulocytes normal
Film: no blasts, no schistocytes, no clumps.
Marrow: normal cellularity with plenty of megakaryocytes.

What is the most likely cause of his low platelets?
questions.e:
Correct: A. A large spleen with mild cytopenias, a normal marrow full of megakaryocytes and no sign of destruction points to sequestration.
B: His marrow is normal and full of megakaryocytes.
C: TTP shows schistocytes and hemolysis.
D: ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion, and the large spleen explains the count.
E: The film shows no clumps.
Takeaway: Low platelets: less production, more destruction, or sequestration.

questions.p:
Bleeding emergencies in two patients:
Patient 1: on warfarin with an intracranial hemorrhage, INR 3.4.
Patient 2: on dabigatran with a major GI bleed.

Which reversal plans fit, in order?
o: Vitamin K IV plus PCC, then protamine sulphate
Vitamin K IV plus PCC, then idarucizumab
Idarucizumab, then vitamin K IV plus PCC
questions.e:
Correct: C. Warfarin emergency reversal = vitamin K plus PCC (vitamin K prevents rebound coagulopathy once PCC wears off). Dabigatran's antidote is idarucizumab, a monoclonal antibody.
A: Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.
B: Protamine has no effect on dabigatran.
D: This reverses the two antidotes.
Takeaway: Andexanet alfa targets Xa inhibitors. Protamine targets UFH (partial for LMWH).

questions.p:
Elaine is on an IV UFH infusion at 1000 units per hour. She develops major bleeding. The infusion has run steadily for 6 hours.

Using the rule in your notes, what dose of protamine sulphate fits best?
questions.e:
Correct: D. Protamine is 1 mg per 100 units of UFH given in the last 2 to 2.5 hours. 1000 U/h x 2.5 h = 2500 U, so 25 mg.
A: 10 mg covers only 1 hour of infusion.
B: 60 mg counts all 6 hours. UFH from earlier has already cleared (half-life 60 to 90 minutes).
C: 100 mg is the maximum single dose. Too much causes hypotension and a weak anticoagulant effect.
Takeaway: Only recent heparin counts because of the short half-life.

questions.p: Which precaution is NOT recommended for a child with hemophilia?
o: Avoid antiplatelet agents such as aspirin
Use prophylactic factor infusions at home
Wear a helmet when riding a bicycle
questions.e:
Correct: A. Routine dental care is recommended because it prevents the need for dental surgery.
B: Avoiding aspirin is recommended.
C: Home infusion prophylaxis is the norm in Canada for severe hemophilia.
D: Protective gear is recommended.
Takeaway: Primary prophylaxis prevents joint bleeds and has improved life expectancy.

questions.p: Which of the following is NOT an adverse effect or limitation of unfractionated heparin?
questions.e:
Correct: B. UFH is degraded by the RES in the liver and is safe in renal failure. LMWH is the one that accumulates.
A: Osteoporosis is an adverse event of UFH.
C: HIT is an adverse event of UFH, about 3 times more than with LMWH.
D: UFH is heterogeneous with unpredictable pharmacokinetics.
Takeaway: LMWH vs UFH: less bleeding, less HIT, less osteoporosis, home treatment, but renal clearance.

questions.p:
A lab technologist runs a PT and an aPTT on the same citrated plasma sample.

Which reagent component is present in the PT test but absent from the aPTT test?
questions.e:
Correct: A. PT reagent contains thromboplastin (tissue factor), which drives the extrinsic pathway via FVII. The aPTT reagent has no tissue factor.
B: Both tests add calcium chloride to overcome citrate.
C: Both reagents contain phospholipid.
D: The contact activator belongs to the aPTT, not the PT.
Takeaway: PT = TF-driven (VII, then X, V, II, I). aPTT = contact-driven (XII, XI, IX, VIII, then common).

questions.p:
Margaret, 78, has 3 weeks of large spontaneous bruises on her arms and thighs and a bleed into her forearm muscle. She never bled with past surgeries or childbirth. She takes no anticoagulants and has no family history of bleeding.

Hb 98 g/L (ref 115-160)
Platelets 260 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR normal
aPTT prolonged
50:50 mixing study aPTT does not correct
FVIII activity very low

What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Acquired hemophilia A from an FVIII inhibitor
questions.e:
Correct: E. New, severe bleeding in an older adult with no past bleeding, an isolated long aPTT that does not correct on mixing, and very low FVIII fit an acquired inhibitor against FVIII. Correction means a deficiency, while no correction means an inhibitor.
A: Congenital hemophilia shows up in childhood, and the mixing study would correct.
B: Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the INR first.
C: Factor XII deficiency doesn't cause bleeding.
D: Type 1 VWD causes mucosal bleeding, and the mixing study would correct.
Takeaway: Acquired bleeding disorders include hemophilia A, VWD and platelet disorders.

questions.p:
Noah, 10, has had two knee bleeds after soccer and a large thigh hematoma after a fall. His mother's brother has a bleeding disorder. He has no nosebleeds or gum bleeding.

Hb 124 g/L (ref 115-155)
Platelets 300 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR normal
aPTT prolonged
50:50 mixing study aPTT corrects
FVIII activity normal
vWF antigen and activity normal

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Joint and muscle bleeds in a boy with an affected maternal uncle, a long aPTT that corrects on mixing, and normal FVIII and vWF point to hemophilia B, factor IX deficiency.
A: Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT/INR.
B: Type 1 VWD causes mucosal bleeding and a low vWF.
C: An inhibitor would not correct on mixing.
D: Hemophilia A would have a low FVIII.
Takeaway: Hemophilia A and B are both X-linked and mostly affect males.

questions.p:
Two boys with severe hemophilia (baseline level near 0%) have joint bleeds. Each needs a target factor level of 60%.
Boy 1 has hemophilia A. Boy 2 has hemophilia B.

Using the rule in your notes (1 U/kg FVIII raises the level by 2%, 1 U/kg FIX raises it by 1%), what dose does each need, in order?
questions.e:
Correct: D. 60% divided by 2% per U/kg = 30 U/kg FVIII. 60% divided by 1% per U/kg = 60 U/kg FIX.
A: This multiplies by 2 instead of dividing.
B: This swaps the recovery rates.
C: FIX recovery is half that of FVIII, so FIX needs double.
Takeaway: Joint bleeds target over 50%.

questions.p:
Consider these statements about heparin-induced thrombocytopenia:
i) It presents with thrombosis, not bleeding
ii) Onset is typically 5 to 10 days after heparin starts
iii) Platelet transfusion is standard treatment
iv) An anti-PF4 ELISA supports the diagnosis

Which are correct?
questions.e:
Correct: C. HIT antibodies form against the heparin-PF4 complex and activate platelets, causing thrombosis. Onset is 5 to 10 days. Anti-PF4 ELISA and the serotonin assay support it.
A: Includes iii). Platelet transfusions are avoided in HIT.
B: Includes iii) and drops ii).
D: Leaves out iv), which is true.
E: iii) is false.
Takeaway: HIT pathophysiology: antibody to heparin-PF4 activates platelets, causing consumption and thrombosis.

questions.p:
Leila, 19, has had nosebleeds since childhood, heavy periods and bleeding gums. Her parents are first cousins. She takes no NSAIDs or other drugs.

Hb 108 g/L (ref 115-160)
Platelets 250 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Platelet size normal
PT/INR normal
aPTT normal
vWF antigen and activity normal
Platelet aggregometry: platelets adhere to collagen but do not aggregate.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: B. Mucocutaneous bleeding with normal platelet number and size, normal clotting tests, normal vWF, and platelets that adhere but fail to aggregate fit Glanzmann thrombasthenia. Aggregation needs GPIIb/IIIa.
A: Bernard Soulier is a disorder of adhesion.
C: Hemophilia A prolongs the aPTT and causes joint bleeds.
D: Her vWF is normal.
E: Her platelet count is normal.
Takeaway: Normal INR and PTT don't rule out a bleeding disorder.

questions.p:
Consider these genetic bleeding disorders:
i) Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a disorder of primary hemostasis
ii) Hemophilia B is a disorder of secondary hemostasis
iii) Type 3 vWD is a disorder of primary hemostasis that also lowers FVIII
iv) Bernard Soulier syndrome is a disorder of secondary hemostasis

Which are correct?
questions.e:
Correct: C. Glanzmann and Bernard Soulier are platelet disorders (primary). Hemophilia B is FIX (secondary). vWD is primary, and type 3 also loses FVIII.
A: Leaves out iii), which is true.
B: Includes iv) and drops iii).
D: Includes iv). Bernard Soulier is a platelet adhesion disorder.
E: iv) is false.
Takeaway: Platelets and vWF = primary. Coagulation factors = secondary.

questions.p: Which patient has the strongest indication for a thrombophilia screen?
o: A 28 year old with unprovoked cerebral vein thrombosis
A 72 year old with DVT after knee arthroplasty
A 60 year old with DVT during chemotherapy
A 70 year old with PE after a long hospitalization
questions.e:
Correct: A. Indications include idiopathic events, age under 55 and unusual location such as the brain. She meets all three.
B: Arthroplasty is a strong provoking factor, and he is over 55.
C: Cancer explains the clot, and she is over 55.
D: Hospitalization is a provoking factor, and he is over 55.
Takeaway: Thrombophilias: FV Leiden, prothrombin mutation, protein C, S, antithrombin deficiency, antiphospholipid antibodies.

questions.p: Which anticoagulant is indirect (needs antithrombin) and inhibits only Factor Xa?
questions.e:
Correct: B. Fondaparinux is a synthetic pentasaccharide that binds antithrombin and inhibits Xa.
A: UFH needs antithrombin but inhibits IIa, Xa, IXa, XIa and XIIa.
C: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor.
D: Rivaroxaban inhibits Xa directly without antithrombin.
Takeaway: Thrombin inhibition needs at least 18 saccharides to bridge antithrombin and thrombin.

questions.p:
During the propagation phase of coagulation, large amounts of Factor Xa are produced.

Which complex converts Factor X to Xa in this phase?
o: Factor Xa with Va, calcium and phospholipid
questions.e:
Correct: D. In propagation, IXa plus VIIIa forms the tenase complex, which converts more X to Xa.
A: TF/VIIa activates only a small amount of IX and X in the initiation phase.
B: This is the prothrombinase complex. It converts prothrombin to thrombin, downstream of Xa.
C: Thrombin activates XIII to cross-link fibrin. It does not form a complex that activates X.
Takeaway: Initiation = TF/VIIa (small burst). Propagation = tenase (IXa/VIIIa) then prothrombinase (Xa/Va).

questions.p:
Two patients have prolonged PT and aPTT.
Patient 1: platelets normal, D-dimer normal, fibrinogen normal, FV normal, FVII low.
Patient 2: platelets low, D-dimer high, fibrinogen low, all factors low.

Which diagnoses fit, in order?
o: Vitamin K deficiency, then liver disease
questions.e:
Correct: A. Patient 1 has a low vitamin K factor (FVII) with normal FV, which is not vitamin K dependent. Patient 2 shows consumption: low platelets, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer and all factors down.
B: This reverses the two patterns.
C: Liver disease lowers FV and fibrinogen. Patient 1 has normal FV and fibrinogen.
D: Liver disease does not raise D-dimer or give low platelets with global consumption, and FVIII rises in liver disease.
Takeaway: FV is the tiebreaker: normal in vitamin K deficiency, low in liver disease and DIC.

questions.p: Which statement about consent for blood transfusion is correct?
o: Verbal consent without any documentation is sufficient
Consent is waived if need is urgent and no SDM is available
Consent covers the procedure and risks only, not alternatives
Consent is waived whenever the patient is over 80
questions.e:
Correct: B. Consent is written, explains procedure, risks, benefits and alternatives in a capable patient, and is documented. It is waived in urgent need without an SDM.
A: Consent is written and documented.
C: Alternatives belong in the discussion.
D: Age alone is not a reason to waive consent.
Takeaway: Transfusion steps: need, consent, then blood bank tests (group, screen, crossmatch).

questions.p: Why does warfarin need 5 to 7 days of overlap with UFH or LMWH when treatment starts?
o: Heparin is needed to prevent warfarin-induced HIT
The liver must first convert it into a direct thrombin inhibitor
It blocks antithrombin, and antithrombin takes several days to clear
Its effect reflects lower thrombin, and Factor II has a long half-life
questions.e:
Correct: D. Warfarin blocks synthesis of II, VII, IX, X, protein C and S. Existing factors decay at their own half-lives, and the full effect depends on falling thrombin (II, 60 to 72 h).
A: HIT is caused by heparin, not warfarin.
B: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K reductase (VKORC1). It does not become a thrombin inhibitor.
C: Warfarin does not act on antithrombin. Heparins need antithrombin.
Takeaway: FVII falls first (3 to 8 h), so the INR rises before full protection.

questions.p:
A pregnant patient on therapeutic LMWH needs her anticoagulant effect checked.

Which test fits best?
questions.e:
Correct: C. LMWH has a high anti-Xa to anti-IIa ratio, so it barely affects the aPTT. Monitor anti-Xa directly in pregnancy and renal failure.
A: The aPTT monitors UFH, not LMWH.
B: TT detects thrombin inhibition, which LMWH has little of.
D: INR monitors warfarin.
Takeaway: UFH = aPTT 2 to 4 times daily. LMWH = no routine monitoring, anti-Xa if needed.

questions.p:
Frank, 66, is on day 8 of subcutaneous unfractionated heparin after a hip replacement. His left calf is now swollen, and ultrasound shows a new DVT. He has no bleeding and no fever, and his wound is clean.

Hb 116 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 8.8 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 90 (was 250 before surgery) × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR normal
Fibrinogen normal
Film: no schistocytes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. A platelet fall of more than half, 5 to 10 days into heparin, with a new clot and no bleeding fits HIT. Antibodies against the heparin-PF4 complex activate platelets.
A: ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion and doesn't cause thrombosis.
B: Sequestration needs an enlarged spleen and develops slowly.
C: DIC raises the INR and lowers fibrinogen.
D: TTP shows schistocytes and hemolysis.
Takeaway: Confirm with an anti-PF4 ELISA and a functional serotonin assay.

questions.p:
Diane, 38, is brought in confused with a headache and slurred speech that comes and goes. She has had fevers and new bruising for 3 days. She has had no diarrhea, takes no drugs and is not pregnant.

Hb 82 g/L (ref 115-160)
Reticulocytes high
WBC 9.2 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 9 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR normal
Fibrinogen normal
LDH high
Creatinine mildly high
ADAMTS-13 low
Film: many schistocytes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Neurological signs, fever, severe thrombocytopenia, hemolysis with schistocytes, normal clotting tests and a low ADAMTS-13 fit TTP. Ultra-large vWF multimers go uncut and cause clotting.
A: DIC raises the INR and lowers fibrinogen.
B: HIT needs heparin exposure and causes thrombosis.
C: HUS follows a diarrheal illness and has a normal ADAMTS-13.
D: ITP has no hemolysis or schistocytes.
Takeaway: TTP: plasma exchange and steroids. Avoid platelet transfusions.

questions.p:
Three children present to clinic.
Child 1: 2 year old boy with a swollen knee after a minor fall and easy bruising.
Child 2: 13 year old girl with heavy periods and iron deficiency anemia.
Child 3: 4 year old with petechiae after a viral illness, platelets 6.

Which diagnoses are most likely, in order?
questions.e:
Correct: B. Hemarthrosis in a toddler boy suggests hemophilia. Menorrhagia with iron deficiency suggests vWD. Isolated severe thrombocytopenia after a virus suggests ITP.
A: Menorrhagia is a vWF pattern, and petechiae with low platelets fits ITP.
C: Joint bleeding points to factors, not vWF.
D: This reverses the first and last cases.
Takeaway: Petechiae = platelets. Joints = hemophilia. Epistaxis and menorrhagia = vWD.

questions.p:
Consider these statements about antiplatelet agents:
i) Aspirin inhibits cyclooxygenase and lowers thromboxane A2
ii) Clopidogrel blocks the P2Y12 receptor pathway
iii) Abciximab blocks GPIb/IX and prevents platelet adhesion
iv) Abciximab is directed against GPIIb/IIIa and prevents aggregation

Which statements are correct?
questions.e:
Correct: A. Aspirin hits cyclooxygenase (less TXA2). Clopidogrel hits P2Y12. Abciximab targets GPIIb/IIIa and blocks aggregation, so iii) is false.
B: This includes iii). Abciximab targets GPIIb/IIIa, not GPIb/IX.
C: This includes iii) and drops iv).
D: This leaves out iv), which is true.
E: iii) is false, so not all statements hold.
Takeaway: Three drugs, three targets: COX (aspirin), P2Y12 (clopidogrel), GPIIb/IIIa (abciximab).

questions.p:
Mia, 3, had bloody diarrhea for 4 days after a family barbecue. The diarrhea has settled, but she now looks pale and puffy and has passed very little urine for a day. She is not confused and has no rash.

Hb 74 g/L (ref 110-140)
WBC 12.4 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 52 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR normal
Fibrinogen normal
Creatinine high
ADAMTS-13 normal
Film: schistocytes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. A young child with a diarrheal prodrome, then hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, low platelets, acute kidney injury and a normal ADAMTS-13 has HUS, most often from Shiga toxin from E. coli O157:H7.
A: TTP has a low ADAMTS-13 and more neurological signs.
B: ALL shows blasts and doesn't cause schistocytes.
C: ITP has no hemolysis or kidney injury.
D: DIC raises the INR and lowers fibrinogen.
Takeaway: HUS: supportive care. Avoid antibiotics and platelet transfusions.

questions.p: A man has a very long aPTT and a normal PT, but had a tonsillectomy and two dental extractions with no bleeding. Which deficiency best explains this?
o: Factor VII deficiency affecting the extrinsic pathway
A lupus anticoagulant directed against phospholipid-bound proteins
Factor XII deficiency with no bleeding risk
Mild hemophilia A from Factor VIII deficiency
questions.e:
Correct: C. Correction on mixing means a factor deficiency. A long aPTT with a bleed-free surgical history points to a contact factor. Contact factors profoundly elevate the aPTT but do not cause bleeding.
A: FVII deficiency prolongs the PT, not the aPTT.
B: An inhibitor such as a lupus anticoagulant does not correct on mixing.
D: FVIII deficiency also corrects on mixing, but tonsillectomy and extractions without bleeding argue against it.
Takeaway: Mixing: corrects = deficiency, no correction = inhibitor.

questions.p: Which pairing of a natural regulator of hemostasis with its target is correct?
o: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor: Factors V and VIII
Protein C and Protein S: Factors V and VIII
questions.e:
Correct: D. Protein C and S block amplification by targeting FV and FVIII.
A: PAI-1 inhibits t-PA and plasmin, a fibrinolysis regulator.
B: Antithrombin binds IX, X and XI (and thrombin), blocking thrombin already generated.
C: TFPI blocks initiation by targeting TF-VIIa and Xa.
Takeaway: TFPI = initiation. Protein C/S = V and VIII. Antithrombin = thrombin, IX, X, XI.

questions.p:
Sofia, 7, has had bleeding into her right ankle after a minor twist, nosebleeds needing packing, and prolonged bleeding after losing baby teeth. Both parents have mild nosebleeds. She is a girl, and no male relatives have hemophilia.

Hb 110 g/L (ref 110-140)
Platelets 280 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR normal
aPTT prolonged
vWF antigen nearly undetectable
vWF activity nearly undetectable
FVIII activity low

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Almost absent vWF with a low FVIII causes both mucosal and joint bleeding. That is type 3 VWD, the rare severe form, since vWF normally protects FVIII.
A: Type 2 is qualitative, with vWF antigen present.
B: FXIII deficiency has a normal aPTT.
C: Type 1 is a partial deficiency with milder bleeding.
D: Hemophilia A is X-linked and has normal vWF.
Takeaway: vWF adheres platelets to collagen and carries FVIII.
